utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Mr. McCloskey, is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Just a couple of housekeeping matters. I have been meaning to and I've forgotten to offer in the revised Obradovic organisation chart, which you'll remember we did some revisions based on his testimony. We've discussed that with Mr. Gajic, and that is -- it's now ready to go. It's 65 ter 7295. I think you had a hard copy that is not quite complete and correct, so if you can throw that away. We can get you another hard copy, if you'd like. We'll have a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was assuming that you would use it with the current witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We actually have a very similar org [phoen] chart helped -- that was helped developed by this witness, so it will be reflective of the other one. Everyone sees these things a little differently, but he'll have it. So this witness will have his own that will come in soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We would like to receive the hard copy of it. That would assist us. And then we will decide about your move to tender it. The Court Usher will be so kind to -- do you have it available at the moment or at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't have the hard copy right now. It should be -- it's not hard. We'll print it right out and it will come very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if he's going to give it a number or not, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We will do that at a later stage, when we have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. And, Mr. President, as you know, the time estimates for this witness have varied. I have had a chance to speak to him now, and it is my hope I can get direct done within two days. He acknowledges he is -- uses a lot of words, and he understands I may interrupt him a bit, but -- and it's very difficult to estimate these things, but I really hope to get this done within two days. And I, as always, invite Your Honours to ask questions. It's such a broad topic that it's hard to always judge specifically your interests. So I have no problem being interrupted, and that's always very helpful when you do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You shouldn't be too optimistic in your estimation, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, that's true. I want to leave myself some room because I really -- it's so hard to tell, though. And, lastly, I would request a caution for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Welcome to the courtroom. Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable. On the request of the Prosecution, I would like to give you a caution. In our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we have the Rule 90(E), and I would like to read it out for you. I quote: "The witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence, other than false testimony." Sir, did you understand what I was reading to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey is now commencing his examination-in-chief and putting questions to you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you please state your name for us.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where were you born?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 21st of November, 1943, in the village of Laminci, the municipality of Gradiska, entity of Bosnia and Herzegovina, state of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, are you currently employed or retired or engaged in something?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a lieutenant general retired for 10 years now. At the moment, I'm a senator of Republika Srpska. That means that, in a way, I'm involved in politics, and I mostly -- I'm dealing with the issues relating to The Hague Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us what your title of your position was throughout the war in Bosnia from 1992 through 1995? Just your simple title, and then we'll get into more details later.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, from the 11th of May, 1992, until the 27th of April, 1997, I was the Chief of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and at the same time I was the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And now can you take just a few minutes and tell us about your military career, just where you first started out, some of your significant promotions, and especially when you first met General Mladic. But if you could just take three, four, five minutes, perhaps, to give us that run-down. I know we could spend a lot longer, and I don't mean to understate your record. But if you could just take a few minutes and tell us, I think that's a good way to start.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I completed my elementary school in 1959, I applied, and it was a miracle that I was accepted into the Military School in Banja Luka for armoured units. I completed that school, and I was sent to the Benkovac Garrison for service, where I spent 14 months as the -- as a non-commissioned officer, commander of a tank platoon. Then I went to the Military Academy of the Land Army --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As you know, you're being translated, and I can tell the translator is having a bit of a hard time, so if you could slow down. It will be a little unnatural, but especially let's -- you and I need to get a good pace, because it will get more difficult as we go.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise. I completed the Military Academy in September 1966, and I remained in service in the Banja Luka Garrison, where I stayed until 1975, when I was sent for additional training to the so-called Higher Military Academy or the General Staff School for Tactics, where I spent two years. I completed that school in 1977, and then I was transferred to duties in the Prilep Garrison in Macedonia, where I stayed for slightly less than four years. Then I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, sorry for interrupting. Can you tell us what rank you started out in, in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I went to Macedonia as captain first class. And then in Prilep, I was promoted to major in September 1979. In early January 1981, I was transferred to the Titov Velez Garrison. Actually, in Prilep I was commander of the armoured battalion. In Velez, I became an operative in the motorised brigade. I stayed in Velez for nine years, and in 1986/1987 I completed the Operations School or War School. I completed that training, and I returned to the Velez Garrison and was appointed commander of the 212th Motorised Brigade. I stayed at that post for some two and a half years, and then later --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, I'm sorry. Could you tell us what rank you held when you were commander of that post?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As an operative, I held the rank of major until 1984, when I was promoted to lieutenant-colonel. And as lieutenant-colonel, I went to complete the War School training. When I returned from school, I assumed duties in the already-mentioned 212th Motorised Brigade, where I remained for two and a half years, approximately. And then in January 1989 I was transferred to the 3rd Army Command or the 3rd Military District in Skopje, where I was the chief of the operations organ or the Operations Administration. In 1990 I was promoted to the rank of colonel, and I stayed at that post until shortly before the withdrawal of the JNA from Macedonia in 1992. Then I was tasked with organising the withdrawal of the combat section of the JNA from Macedonia according to the agreement between the president of the newly-created Republic of Macedonia, Kiro Gligorov, and the Chief of the General Staff of the JNA, General Blagoje Adzic. The condition was for the JNA to withdraw without firing a single bullet, which was done. Shortly before the withdrawal of the JNA, I was appointed as chief of the operations and training organ as a general. I was promoted to the rank of general on the 26th of April, 1992. And on the 8th of May of that same year, I received a degree or, rather, an order for transfer to the Sarajevo Garrison to carry out the same duties that I was carrying out in the 3rd Army Command in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you continue your description until we get up to May 11th and the creation of the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in your previous question, there was a sub-question asking me how long have I known General Ratko Mladic. I met General Mladic when he held the rank of major in April 1981. He was working at the 3rd Army Command at the time, at the training organ, and he came to inspect my brigade. I was assigned to escort him that day. Well, the way we met was not all that great, actually, but later we co-operated very well. Together, we were transferred to the 3rd Army Command. I was transferred there from the Command of the 212th Brigade, and he was transferred there from the duty of the Command of the 39th Brigade in Stip. I mentioned the decree by the SFR -- by the SFRY Presidency on my transfer to Sarajevo. According to that decree, I was to supposed to perform/carry out the same duties in the 2nd Army Command in Sarajevo that I was carrying out in the 3rd Army District. The dead-line for the transfer was the 11th of May, 1992. Previously, I had to report to the General Staff of the JNA, which existed then still, in order to receive the original documents for transfer, for my promotion to the rank of general, and to receive an explanation where I was going and why I was going. I reported to said administration. Well, there was an agreement the previous -- for Ratko Mladic and myself to meet the previous day at the JNA Command. When I arrived, he wasn't there. I reported to the chief of the Personnel Administration, General Gojko Krstic. He gave me these documents, but he also told me about some changes. In the meantime, the Dobrovoljacka incident occurred in Sarajevo on the 3rd of May, when JNA soldiers were victims, and the General Staff of the JNA decided to replace the then commander of the 2nd Military District, General Milutin Kukanjac, and his Chief of Staff. The change in the transfer order was to appoint Mladic as commander of the 2nd Military District, and I was appointed as the Chief of Staff. I objected as to why I was going to Sarajevo when I was told at the time of the decision of the Presidency of the SFRY that the JNA was withdrawing from Bosnia-Herzegovina and it should be done by the 19th of May, meaning that this had to be done in less than eight days. I asked him, Why am I going to Bosnia if the JNA was disappearing from Bosnia? I was told that a helicopter would take me where I'm supposed to go and that General Mladic would explain all the details to me. I flew into some forest. This was Crna Rijeka, some nine kilometres north-east of Han Pijesak. I didn't meet up with Mladic or Kukanjac or that Chief of Staff who I was supposed to replace. Mladic flew in from Herzegovina sometime in the afternoon, towards evening. Since I found out that General Perisic was withdrawing from Herzegovina as part of the JNA forces - up until that time he was in command of the Bileca -- the Herzegovina Corps - I thought that I would probably go to replace Perisic. However, when Mladic flew in, when he landed, this was some 50 metres away from the hut. We crossed this within some 45 minutes or an hour, and he told me during that time what all of this was about. He told me that it was correct --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Let me stop you there and just go back a little bit. You had mentioned that you had worked, I believe, well with General Mladic, but it wasn't clear in what context you were working. Were you in the same unit, were you in neighbouring units? And can you just take a minute or two just to describe for how -- what period of time you worked with him and in what context, prior to the Crna Rijeka helicopter.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, after we met in April 1981, Mladic left the army command soon after that and went to Ohrid to be the commander of the infantry regiment. We would meet during exercises, mostly the joint army exercises. And then I can't remember exactly what year this was, Mladic was transferred when there was a reorganisation of the JNA and when corps were formed. Mladic was transferred to Stip to be the commander of the 39th Infantry Brigade. I was still an operative in the 212th Brigade. Stip and Velez are some 48 kilometres apart. The AORs of our brigades actually touched at Ovca [phoen] and Bregovnice [phoen], so that we had frequent contacts. Mladic would always be one step ahead of me in command and operative duties. However, when we applied for the Operatics [as interpreted] School, the War School, we both found ourselves in Belgrade, he as the brigade commander, and I was still an operative in the brigade. But we did complete this school together. We travelled together from Macedonia to Belgrade and back. We worked together, since we were close. We did our homework together and prepared our seminars for school. When we came back from school, I began my duties in the 212th Brigade, so from that time on we were equals. We co-operated well. But as far as the professional area is concerned, we always had opposite views. Our objectives were the same, but the way to get to that objective was different. So we would often clash on professional matters, and then the chief of the army staff or the army commander would have to reconcile us. Then together we came to the army command, Mladic as the chief of the training organ, and I was the chief of the operations organ in the same operations and training organ. That means that we worked as equals and co-operated in our jobs. The duties of the operations and training organ, among other things, included the training of command superior officers. We would prepare the staff wartime exercises, command staff exercises. When there were problems in Kosovo, the two of us made the plans of the show of force, the replacement of units in Kosovo. We co-operated there together. There were always sparks between us, but we always managed to find a common language. When I learned that I would be Mladic's deputy during the war, I was a little concerned that Mladic would have his revenge on me from everything from the peacetime period. After six months, actually, he explained this by saying that he asked for me to be his deputy, and he literally said this: I ignite in the first gear, and you ignite in the third gear, and the best driving is done in the second gear. So before setting out on an assignment, I would always analyse the consequences. And Mladic always made his decisions much faster, so that he felt that these two temperaments would actually work well together and balance each other out. During the war, we didn't have any problems between us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And now let's go back. I believe it's May 11th when you both meet in Crna Rijeka, and can you briefly tell us about that? Who was there, what happened there? But briefly. We need to, as you know, get to the 1995 period relatively soon.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: As I've said already, I waited for him at the helio-pad. We greeted each other and congratulated each other on our promotions. The same decree pronounced me to major general, pronouncing him to lieutenant general. Forty-five minutes later, we entered one of the two existing barracks. In one room, there were some 10 people waiting for us. There were four generals in total: Mladic, General Djukic, General Gvero, and myself. There was seven colonels and lieutenant-colonels, and one captain first class, Pecanac. Among them was the then Colonel Tolimir. Mladic introduced us. I had known General Gvero from before. He used to be a professor in the Political School of the JNA, which I completed in 1982. I saw General Djukic for the first time. He was an elderly gentleman of aristocratic poise. When Mladic introduced Colonel Tolimir, I may have pulled a face or made an expression because I used to work with another Tolimir in Banja Luka who was Slovenian, and I thought that this Tolimir was a Slovenian too. But Mladic told me, Don't be afraid, he's a greater Serb than you are. Mladic told us that the next day, on the 12th of May, the People's Assembly of the RS would hold a session in Banja Luka, during which a decision was to be made to establish the Army of Republika Srpska. If there were going to be additional explanations as to why the Serbs were establishing their army that late in the war, we can discuss that later. That evening, Mladic explained to us what our respective tasks were. He told me, although these were all assumptions at the time only -- well, he said that I was to -- that he was to command the Main Staff and that I was going to be his Chief of Staff and deputy. Gvero was supposed to be assistant commander for morale and religious issues. Tolimir was to be the chief of the Intelligence and Security Administration. General Djukic was to become his assistant for logistics or, rather, chief of the Logistics Sector. There was another colonel of artillery and rocket units by the name of Krstic who was to withdraw from the JNA by the 19th of May, and he was to be replaced by Colonel Jovo Maric, who was a pilot and was with the Air Force Administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, let me interrupt you. This Court is, of course, familiar with Radislav Krstic, the commander of the Drina Corps. Is this Krstic you've just mentioned a different Krstic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a different Krstic. This Krstic that you are referring to was an infantryman. The one I found in the newly-formed Main Staff was an artillery and rocket units colonel. He was in the Command of the 2nd Army, and we received him that evening, since he was well acquainted with the anti-aircraft and air force defence systems. So it's not the Radislav Krstic you have in mind. On the list for that evening, there was also Colonel Petar Salapura. Mladic told him that he was to be the chief of the Intelligence Administration in the Intelligence and Security Sector. However, he wasn't there that evening because he had already gone to execute a task. We discussed throughout the night. We didn't have the war goals. None of us, save for Mladic and perhaps Tolimir, was in contact with the Presidency of the RS. Therefore, we didn't know why the army was being formed. We could presume, though. It was to be formed as the last armed force in the territory of the former SFRY, the seventh force in a row. We discussed, we made conclusions, we weighed proposals as to what the army should be structured like and what it was to do. We produced 21 conclusions. One of them -- well, they basically laid foundations for the VRS, although I don't remember them all by heart. We also decided on the doctrine, and I believe there were nine goals in total as part of that. First of all, it was supposed to be a defensive armed force. Second, its task was to protect the Serb people and territory. One of the goals was also to liquidate or eliminate the existing paramilitary forces as well as municipal TO units which had been formed by the party in power, the SDS, mostly in the municipalities on the outskirts of our territory, neighbouring majority Muslim and Croatian population municipalities. Crisis staffs were taken out of the system of command of army units, and there was another decision which said that if any of us was to be replaced during the war out of the 12 of us, everyone would leave, that is, if anyone was replaced for political reasons. We decided to go, all of us, in such a case and to go to the trenches to take up arms. It may have been a marketing decision of sorts at the time, but it was also an obligation, an oath we undertook, which kept the homogeneity of the Main Staff throughout the war. It was also thanks to that that the corps commands remained together, because they joined us later on in the execution of those goals. Thanks to that decision, I refused on three occasions to assume General Mladic's position. The next morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you want to get into the next morning, but be brief. Remember -- I know those were very complex and important days in 1992, but go ahead and tell us what happened the next morning, but in brief.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The next morning, everyone flew to Banja Luka to attend the Assembly session. I remained in the Main Staff, however, to set it up and to translate our discussions of the last night into bulletins, information, and orders. I was also in charge of establishing communication and command links with the subordinate units and was supposed to monitor events of that day in the Bosnia-Herzegovina theatre. As for establishing communication links with the subordinate units, I was appalled to learn that the war was already underway, that there was fierce fighting, although the army had not been formed, around Sarajevo, for example. There was also fighting in all municipalities on the outer rim of the RS territory. So when Mladic came back that evening, I told him, Man, we're already at war. By the end of that day, the Main Staff was formed and functional. However, we were still short of staff. In the course of the first few days, we relied on officers from the 2nd Army Command who had fled Sarajevo as they awaited their transfer or withdrawal to Yugoslavia. The gravest problems we had were in Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zenica, because the JNA units there were surrounded, especially in Sarajevo, where the Military Schools Centre of the JNA was under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, General.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Colonel Ljubisa Beara join the Main Staff at some point that year?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ljubisa Beara, as a naval captain, he used to be in the navy, but he was an equal to a colonel in the land forces. He joined us in September of 1991 -- 1992, although I am not positive. In any case, I think it was in early September. He was introduced to us by General Mladic. The two of them were walking around the buildings there. When I came, I could see that they had known each other. And Mladic told me that Beara worked in Split before the war, and in the Main Staff he was supposed to be chief of the Security Administration in the Intelligence and Security Sector. Therefore, we met that day and agreed that any security issues that I had as the Chief of Staff should be dealt with through Colonel Tolimir, who was chief of the Intelligence and Security Sector. In other words, I was not supposed to have direct contact with the chief of the Intelligence and Security Administration. However, that had to be done later on because of the nature of work I performed, which was planning operations, and I always needed latest information on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. Judge Mindua would like to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we move on [indiscernible] [microphone not activated]. There's one point I would like to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Okay, good. [Interpretation] On the transcript, page 14, line 20 to 23, you say that the war had already begun. The Army of the Republika Srpska had not been established yet. Since you attended the meeting in Banja Luka before the establishment of the Army of the Republika Srpska, who was actually waging a war in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm afraid there's still a problem with the microphone, perhaps in the interpreter's booth for French. I don't think that this is a problem here on the Bench for the Judges. Now it seems to be better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: Okay, I will try again. [Interpretation] On the transcript, page 14, lines 20 to 23, you said that the decision to establish the Army of the Republika Srpska was taken at the Assembly meeting in Banja Luka on the following day, but you also said that the war had already started in Sarajevo. What I would like to know is: Who was fighting who in Sarajevo? Who was waging a war at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, I said so, although I must say I understood your question the first time around. There was no need for me, at least, to have it repeated. When mobilisation was proclaimed by the Muslim-Croat coalition on the 4th of April, it meant that on that day the armed forces of the Muslims and Croats were formed. The Presidency of the RS responded by proclaiming the so-called immediate threat of war. It organised its Territorial Defence units in the areas neighbouring Muslim and Croat territories. On the evening of the 11th of May, on the eve of the Assembly session, we had between 80- and 90.000 people who had arms. At least that was the information Mladic gave us. They were organised in two different types of structure or organisation. The first one were TO units which were formed ad hoc in the various municipalities. The second structure, which was smaller in size, were the various paramilitary units, which were mainly introduced from or came from Serbia and Montenegro. I have already told you what we decided to do with those paramilitary units. As for the TO units in the municipalities, they were engaged in combat whenever the population of a village or town came under attack. Those brigades responded to attacks, to challenges. They were headed by only a few professional officers who were mainly reserve officers and also members or people from the party in power. They mainly operated under the command of municipal war staffs. At the outset of my testimony, I told you that one of the decisions of the Main Staff was to remove that right of command from the municipal staffs. Before we became engaged in the war, the war was waged exclusively by these TO units which were there to protect the population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood you correctly, these TO units were, in fact, Serb units. They were protecting the Serb population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were predominantly Serb units or units comprising Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, going back to something you said, I was not exactly clear. You said that initially you were not supposed to have direct contact with someone, but I'm not clear on who that was. Can you explain that again to me, briefly?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: You mean when we discussed Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you were discussing the Security and Intel Branch and your position, that initially you were to have restricted contact with someone, but it came out sounding a little different. So could you just explain that? I'm not sure we got the translation correct.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did think of that. I may have misspoken. In principle, command and control excludes the possibility of a general or an officer having direct contact or co-operation with his subordinate two levels down. The only need I had was to contact with the Security or Intelligence Service which were in Tolimir's sector. In doing so, I didn't go through his chiefs of administration; I went straight through Tolimir, who was chief of sector. And then it was up to him whether he would assign a particular task to the chief of his Security or Intelligence Administration. The principle of command and control is that one does not issue commands to his subordinate two levels down. As opposed to that, I was supposed to meet Karadzic's orders, who was two steps up. This is another principle. But upon receipt of such an order, I had to report it to General Mladic. By the same token, the chief of the Security Administration, if he had an urgent matter to communicate to me, he could, but he also had to acquaint Colonel Tolimir with having done so, with getting in touch with me. So this is a principle of subordination so as I could not meddle in Tolimir's work or he in mine. That's it. Since when, on the first day, I saw Beara, I could see that he was an imposing person, so to say, and under such circumstances I told him I was not going to co-operate directly with him but that we would communicate through Tolimir. For the most part, it was so, although we did some direct contact in relation to front-line issues. Even if we did so, it always had to be with the approval or knowledge of General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we will get into those command and subordinated relationships a bit more, but thank you for that fundamental part. Did that fundamental principle that you've just described remain throughout the wartime period?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, I know you have helped the investigation -- or the investigator work out what we refer to as the VRS structure, showing the commander, the units, the various positions, and I'm going to get to that with you to help us understand it. I'm not going to spend a lot of detail on that. The Judges have heard from other officers much of the basics, but I will go into that with you some. But before we get there, can you just take a couple of minutes and describe how the structure worked in 1995, basically? And what I mean by that is: Can you start with Karadzic, the supreme commander, and what authority he had, and then go to Mladic, your position, the assistant commanders, and the various corps and other units? Can you just give us just a brief on how that structure worked and how the authorities worked, starting with Radovan Karadzic? And this would be for 1995.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. As early as 1995, Radovan Karadzic became well versed in his role of supreme commander because by that time he had spent some three years in that position. At the outset, it wasn't quite clear to him that he couldn't issue orders directly to me or to a corps commander, but that all of his orders had to go through Ratko Mladic and then down to his subordinates. These were some initial mistakes, which were understandable because he was not a military professional. By 1995, he no longer made such mistakes unless he really intended to do so. There are stories/rumours about the relationship between Karadzic and Mladic. I don't know whether we will touch upon that topic. It very much depends on you. But in 1995, Karadzic had a circle of stable military advisers around him who made proposals to him at the strategic level. Unfortunately, none of the advisers was trained and educated as well as the Main Staff. They did not have the breadth of military expert knowledge, and frequently they suggested to Karadzic things that did not play out, in military terms. There was no military logic in it. For example, I received an order that the VRS in the next 24 hours was to occupy a town. First of all, that town was not even in the RS. Second, to occupy a larger settlement in 24 hours would require at least a week's preparation. In other words, their proposals were unprofessional. In 1994, when making such decisions, Karadzic began consulting with us from the Main Staff before making a decision. Such consultations were supposed to be done in the Ministry of Defence, but even the Ministry of Defence lacked trained personnel for such affairs, especially since the minister of defence was a civilian, unlike before. But already in 1995, but one may say even as of April 1994, with the beginning of the NATO air-strikes, Karadzic started thinking more deeply about military decisions. And during 1995, the co-operation with him was very good, up until July or August 1995 when he again started meddling with the work of the Main Staff and the authorities of the commander of the Main Staff. I'm sure we will come to that during your examination. General Mladic -- I don't know who hasn't had this bit of comment on General Mladic, and I was also one of those people who had a lot to say about him. He was a commander by nature, I cannot say from birth, but he had charisma, he was persistent, decisive, a man who, whenever he could or, rather, whenever it was necessary, so a man who protected his subordinates. He was a role model for his subordinated officers, commanders of corps and brigades and so on. During the war, he would not reach rash decisions, and he would not reach decisions without having consulted the Main Staff, up until mid 1994, when he did reach a few decisions on his own, mostly because he wanted to achieve something quickly, successfully. But very often, it didn't work. At the time of the end of the war, he started having kidney problems. He did not, however, spend much time in hospitals. His illness was something that he had to live with in command posts and on the battle-fields, and we understood that and we tried to assist people, and the army had unlimited confidence in him. If there were any conflicts between him and Karadzic, and they were never direct, of course, these conflicts were along the lines of who's going to be the first man in the state, both of them very charismatic, both of them had great hunger for power. And they had problems in understanding each other, but it would eventually happen. And Mladic was duty-bound, of course, because of the structure of the army, to carry out the government's decisions. And let me just add, to avoid any confusion later on: I wrote to you about how the Supreme Command of the Republika Srpska was formed or established. Bearing in mind its composition, one can see that it was a civilian body in charge of waging the war. Mr. Karadzic, President Karadzic, was the supreme commander, as the Constitution provided for, and the command also included two presidents, presidents of the Assembly or speaker of the Assembly and the prime minister. Do you want me to tell their names?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For 1995. Anything that's applicable for 1995, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. The president of the Assembly in 1995 and throughout the war, as a matter of fact, was Momcilo Krajisnik. And in 1995, the prime minister was Dusan Kozic, until, in late 1995, he was replaced by Gojko Klickovic. No, I apologise, first by Rajko Kasagic and then by Gojko Klickovic. In 1995, we had three prime ministers, and they were immediately members of the Supreme Command because of their duty. Then minister of defence who was also a member, Milan Ninkovic; and the minister of the interior, I think at the time it was Tomo Kovac, because the ministers of interior changed very often, but I think then it was Tomo Kovac. There were also two vice-presidents of the republic who were at some stage also included into the Supreme Command, Koljevic and Plavsic. In the Supreme Command, there was no one from --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. Yesterday, we heard the name of, I think, Koljevic as a -- can you spell that name out, the vice-president person that you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nikola Koljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd interrupted you, but had you just -- I think you'd just about finished that thought.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No one from the Supreme Command, with the exception of Karadzic, had the authority of -- had the order-issuing authority; only Karadzic. All links between the Main Staff and the Supreme Command went through Karadzic. Members of the Supreme Command could make proposals, but Karadzic was the one who was making all the decisions. We never carried out orders by Krajisnik, Plavsic, or Koljevic, only the directives issued by Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was that established by the Constitution and Law of the RS, Karadzic's authority to issue the orders to you? When I say "you," I mean the Main Staff, Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the Constitution, the president of the republic is also the commander -- the supreme commander of the armed forces. However, the armed forces are not only the military. They comprise of military, the police, and civilian protection. In other words, Karadzic was in command of all these three segments, including the military, the army. Within his Supreme Command, he had people who were in charge of police, mainly the minister of the interior. There was also a person who was in charge of civilian protection. I don't know who he was. I think it may have been the minister of defence. And he was the only one, according to the Constitution, who had any authority over the army, who could command the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, General. So I think that's helpful to give us a primer on the political structures upon which General Mladic was required to follow. Can you just, in a -- and I know this is difficult, but just in one or two minutes describe General Mladic's job. Just what -- and the Judges have heard quite a bit already on this, but can you just tell us what his job was as the commander of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic was the commander of the Main Staff. That was his title; not the commander of the VRS, but the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for correcting me on that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That implied, because the Main Staff is the body commanding the army there, for Mladic, as the commander of the Main Staff, was the commander of the army. So you didn't say it -- you didn't put it wrongly. He was, in fact, the commander of the VRS, but that was not his title, and you couldn't find that in his personal files, for instance, because in conditions of war, in a state that has not yet been recognised internationally and that has not yet been fully organised and that is initiating the struggle for national liberation, one cannot find a main staff, a general staff, because the state has not been established yet. During war, a general staff becomes the staff of the Supreme Command, in fact. So since we were at the beginning, the group of people in charge or leading the armed struggle is called the Supreme Command. Tito, during the war, had a different body, but in different republics, then of course in all the republics of the former Yugoslavia, he had staffs that were in charge of liberating their areas from fascism. In the same manner, we had a Main staff during the war, and the idea was that after the end of the war, the Main Staff would become a General Staff, and that did happen, indeed, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you just, as I said, in one or two minutes, describe what General Mladic's job was. And after that, I'll ask you in the same context, just tell us, as you've partly done, what the job of the Main Staff was, the assistants and the other -- the sectors of the Main Staff, but just generally and simply, just as a primer before we get into the various sectors and describe more particularly what they did. That may be confusing, so let me just -- just two minutes on what General Mladic's job, as commander, was.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The job of General Mladic was, in brief, to command the Main Staff. The Main Staff had 12 tasks. I provided them to you yesterday, starting with the mobilisation of the army, which normally would have been something carried out by the Ministry of Defence. But since the Ministry of Defence was short-staffed, the Supreme Command or, rather, the Presidency of Republika Srpska tasked the Main Staff to carry that out because we did have a Sector for Mobilisation and Replenishment. Furthermore, the Main Staff was in charge of establishing units at all levels, from squads to corps. It was another of our tasks. Furthermore, training of officers and soldiers, in other words, preparing for combat. Then we had another role that should have been the role of the Ministry of Defence, and that was the logistics for the army. Then planning and carrying out combat operations, reporting to the Supreme Command, receipt and processing of reports received from subordinated units, approving or not approving requests from subordinated commands. Or, in short, we did everything in charge -- everything that needs to be done when one's at war. One of the tasks was also security and intelligence support for the army, which was under General Tolimir. Mladic was carrying out orders by the Supreme Command. All of us were carrying out his orders. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say you were all carrying out General Mladic's orders, can you just give us a practical idea of how Mladic commanded? I mean, did he issue orders?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Mladic commanded by using the system or method of meetings. In the Main Staff, we had an institution, the college of commander, commanders' college. The staff would meet -- or collegium. The staff would meet every morning and every evening. Between 6.00 and 7.00, we'd be receiving reports from subordinated commanders, and based on these reports, we would jointly, as the staff, review the situation. We would try and see what needs to be improved, what was good, what needs to be done completely from the scratch. Us seven assistants were giving proposals each for his own sector. The logistics officer, the last one, would brief the staff on the amount of ammunition and to tell us -- and I'll make it -- I'll reduce it to absurd, but how many 7.62-millimetre bullets could be used that day. Then Tolimir would inform us about the security situation in the republic and the intelligence information about the intentions of the enemy and so forth and would give proposals how to counteract that. General Gvero would talk about the morale of the troops. Or if there was a specific unit to -- that was carrying out any task, he would be the one to say, No, this unit can easily carry it out, or, It will have difficulties. The Chief of Staff listens to all the reports and then gives proposals to General Mladic on how to use his troops, be it individual units or the army in total. I, for instance, would tell him, Let us attack this specific hill or cut this specific communication. I have to also tell him what the cost of such an action would be, which was based on having heard all the reports before that. I provide my assessment of the potential casualties on our side, and so on and so forth. And then after having heard us, the General Staff would make a break, and he would keep the most necessary among us for that decision to stay with him and help him in reaching the decision. And about half an hour later he would inform us about his decision. He might, on one hand, tell us, word by word, what needs to be done, or he could say, Well, we'll do what the Chief of Staff had proposed, or someone else. When we were reaching major decisions about activities on operational level, namely, when a corps or more corps are involved, then we would call the corps commanders to the meeting, and that would be the collegium in its extended version. The Main Staff can reach a certain decision, but if the commander Novica Simic of the Eastern Bosnia Corps says we cannot carry it out, then we haven't gotten anywhere. The corps commanders are those who know what their capacities are at the moment, and he can inform the staff if that is possible or not, and then we look for solutions. I think it was only our army that had this feature; namely, that corps-level decisions were reached with the presence of all corps commanders, which had its good consequence, this system. Namely, we wouldn't have to inform other corps commanders, neighbouring corps, for instance, what General Simic's task was because they were there at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask the witness to slow down a little bit. It is very difficult to follow him, especially when one does it the way I do while listening to both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You want to have everything under control. I understand. Please carry on, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, can we just clarify that. These morning -- you've described a morning staff meeting and an evening staff meeting. Can you just make clear for us: Who was at the morning staff meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The morning meetings were in an expanded composition. All the commanders' assistants were also present there, then chiefs of administration. For instance, from Tolimir's sector, we would have three people -- three persons present, Tolimir himself, and two administration chiefs. From my sector, there would be the chief of Training and Operations Administration, and General Miletic could also bring his assistants, chief of Operational Department and the other one. So the meetings involved the first and the second level of the staff, including commanders' assistants and their subordinates. In the evening meetings, because most of the officers would be in their units and maybe last until midnight, they were held at 2.00 -- at 2000 hours and would last for a while. It would definitely include either commander or myself and chiefs of sectors, and in their absence they would have a chief of administration who would replace them; Beara or Salapura, for instance, for Mr. Tolimir. And at that meeting, all those who were practically in the staff would be present, and a duty team which included 10 to 12 officers, mainly representatives of branches and services. At that meeting we would go through daily combat reports received from subordinated units, and we would look for problems. This was usually the last item in their reports. Mainly, it involved logistics, We need ammunition, we need fuel. And then either the logistics officer or the representative of a certain branch would be tasked with making sure that in the morning the required materiel would be available. Extraordinary meetings, there was no need, actually, to have them, but there were some. There were occasions when we'd meet at 4.00 in the morning if the situation at the front-line was critical. The Main Staff --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me clarify something. Pardon me for interrupting. You said the chief of sectors would meet. And when you say "chief of sectors," were those the seven assistant commanders that you spoke of earlier in the formation of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. Chiefs of sectors were at the same time commanders' assistants. Yes, I was the Chief of Staff and at the same time a deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask a question to clarify another issue. You told us that the meetings in the evening commenced at 2000 hours; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They would commence upon the arrival of daily combat reports received from subordinated units so that we could read them all at once, although these documents were also initially read by the chief of the operations, General Miletic or myself if I were there. So it was possible that at the beginning of the meeting I would tell the commander, There's no need to read everything. General, the problems in the 1st Corps are such and such, in the 2nd Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm only interested in the time, because at page 26, lines 24 to 25, I read: "The staff would meet every morning and every evening. Between 6.00 and 7.00 ..." whatever that means. And later on you said in the evening you met at 2000 hours. Could you clarify that? What was the usual meeting time in the morning and the usual meeting time in the evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The usual time of the meetings held in the morning was, as you said it, between 6.00 and 7.00 in the morning. Usually they would start at 7.00, because at 6.00 we would only receive the reports from the corps. And by 7.00 we would be able to say what was happening in the corps during the night. Initially, the evening meetings were starting at 1800 hours, but the reports from subordinated units were never in time, and we slowly pushed the beginning back. And at some point we started having these meetings as of 2000 hours because by 2000 hours all the meetings -- all the reports were in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think just one more question before the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, how consistent was General Mladic in having these meetings? I mean, when he was there, did he always have them or was it a haphazard thing?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When he was present at the staff, he would hold them on a regular basis. If he was absent, if he was somewhere away from the staff, then I would be chairing the meetings, but he never skipped a meeting. Even if there was nothing to discuss, we would meet just to keep the habit going, because you skip one meeting and then maybe we subordinates would start not appearing at meetings, and God knows what, but the meetings were held regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Just to clarify -- I see we still have a minute. And I don't want to -- we'll get into 1995 and where you were a lot of the time later. But in a situation where General Mladic isn't there and you're not there, would there be someone that would normally chair the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If neither General Mladic nor myself were at the staff, the meetings should have been chaired by one of the commanders' assistants; Gvero if it involves issues related to morale, Tolimir if it's related to security, Djukic if it's in relation to logistics. But they were mostly chaired by my assistant, because Operational Sector is a place where all reports come in, all data come in. And if sometimes it would happen that it's necessary -- and I do know that Miletic, who was my deputy and chief of Operational Administration, he was the one chairing the meeting. There was no problem in hierarchy if you would have chief of one sector reporting to a deputy, because he's reporting to the staff, not to the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I see it's the time for the break, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We must have our first break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please carry on. Mr. Gajic. Sorry, I didn't see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a brief comment. I don't think it's a contentious issue, but it didn't get entered into the transcript properly. Page 23, line 10, in the last part: [In English] "No one from --" [Interpretation] That there was nobody from the Main Staff and that General Mladic was not a member of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand. Could you please repeat your comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer given by the witness wasn't interpreted fully, because he said that not a single officer from the Main Staff was a member of the Supreme Command and that General Mladic also was not a member of the Supreme Command. That was untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to invite Mr. McCloskey to clarify that in the course of his examination. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, to clarify that point, is it correct that no officer from the Main Staff or General Mladic was a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The Main Staff was against it, and the corps commands were also against it, because initially the Supreme Command didn't even include the vice-presidents of the republic, Koljevic and Plavsic, and it was only upon the intervention by the army that the vice-presidents were appointed to enter the Supreme Command, nor was General Mladic in the Supreme Command. And we did not ask for General Mladic to become part of the Supreme Command because of our pride, but because the fact that General Mladic was not in the Supreme Command was something that had caused huge problems in the hierarchy of command. Because Mladic was not in the Supreme Command, the Main Staff could not be the staff of Supreme Command, which is something that happens in any army during wartime. The General Staff becomes the Staff of Supreme Command, becomes its integral part, and then you don't have the problems I told you about earlier; namely, that the Supreme Command didn't have professional expertise to draft orders and make decisions. It was done by the supreme commander, and he used his assistants. And that was a problem throughout the entire war. The conflict between the Supreme Command and the Main Staff was caused by the fact that the Main Staff was not an organisational unit of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I ask you, Who else, besides the president and the vice-president, was a member of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The members of the Supreme Command, in addition to the president and the vice-president, were the president of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, president -- or, rather, prime minister of Republika Srpska, the minister of interior of Republika Srpska, and defence minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I forgot you have explained that already earlier. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, going back briefly about the daily meetings, I believe you said that you would -- at times, there would be a second meeting with this smaller group, where the decisions were made or formulated. Can you tell us, that smaller group, who was normally a member of that smaller group that met with General Mladic, if I have that correctly? And, again, 1995 period.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Those meetings were attended with a narrow Main Staff officers, meaning the commander and his assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And since you've started discussing these sectors, specifically you started talking about General Miletic as the chief of operations and training, let's go to the organisational chart that you have recently looked at with the investigator. And that is 65 ter 7397.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is revised from the original that was on the 65 ter list of 65 ter 660, so this is a recent proofing note revision of what's very similar to the older one that did have a proper number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, this is always very awkward, because we try to show on one page the whole -- well, the structure of the whole army. And if we could provide the Court, of course, with the one that General Milovanovic has reviewed, and I have a B/C/S -- a Serbian version for the general because this really doesn't work. It's hard enough to see on paper; you need, practically, a magnifying-glass. But we do want to have one way to see it all, just so we can see it all like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Will it be on the screen or do we receive a hard copy of that as well? No, we are dealing now with the one we just received?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. I hope you received the one that General Milovanovic -- we have General Obradovic's, but I don't want to mix you up with that one yet. That's coming a little later. And General Tolimir and Mr. Gajic should have copies as well. We'd provided them a little bit earlier. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, did you receive a copy, a hard copy, of the chart?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I greet everyone here. May God's peace reign in this house, and may God's will be done in this proceeding and not mine. I want to say hello to General Milovanovic. And, yes, my assistant received the chart, if that's the one that had been reviewed by General Milovanovic, and I can have it, yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, as I said, I don't want to go through every box and every name. But, first of all, we see, of course, as the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, and you've discussed that. We could have also put on this chart President Karadzic and the Supreme Command, but that's not there. But you've discussed that, so I won't go into that any further. But let me -- we see on this box, it goes sideways to the right, the Department of Civil Affairs, and that seems to be set out from everything else. Can you explain what that department is and why it would be set out like this? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters' notes: We do not have the chart. Could we please have it? It would be very useful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, it should appear on the screen. And if there are hard copies left, they should be given to the interpreters, if that is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that's absolutely correct, and we do have some for them. But let's see what it looks like on the chart. With some fancy footwork, we'll be able to blow up the parts that we're talking about. So if we could blow up that top part. But I have these -- I have Serbian versions as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think only the top part would be sufficient at the moment. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, General, just briefly, this department, it's listed as Department for Civil Affairs, and it's got Colonel Milos Djurdjic and Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Kralj. Where does this -- how does it fit into the structure?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: This department was established later in the history of the Main Staff. Up until 1994, decisions on movement and access of humanitarian convoys into enclaves and into Sarajevo was reached by -- were reached by the Main Staff. I think it was General Tolimir who was receiving requests from the UNPROFOR Command, and he would then forward such requests either to me or to the commander in most cases, including his proposal as to whether they should or should not be approved. But in 1994 a commission was formed attached to the Government of Republika Srpska, a commission for humanitarian aid, and it was not the Main Staff who would decide whether humanitarian convoys should be authorised to enter or not. I think the chair of this commission was the vice-president Mr. Nikola Koljevic. He was the one deciding whether a convoy would be allowed to enter Srebrenica or not. If he would decide that they should be let through, he would inform us about it, and the Main Staff was in charge of then stopping all combat activities that were happening along the route of the convoy. Milos Djurdjic entered that department. I don't know where he was before, after the establishment. And Slavko Kralj worked in a similar department in the 1st Corps and was just transferred to the Main Staff. He spoke English really well, and that was the reason, I think, that he became part of this newly-formed department. The chief of the department, Colonel Djurdjic, then was present at joint meetings with UNPROFOR when decisions were made about how many convoys would be allowed, and it remained the duty of the army to make sure that convoys have safe passage and to control whether the goods that are stated in the documentation accompanying the convoy was the only material carried by the convoy, so that we could avoid, for instance, situations where different stuff would be smuggled in like it happened during Operation Parachute. And, now, why is this separately placed here and linked up with General Mladic directly? I think it's because it was added later and they didn't know how to graphically put it in differently. Many of the requests would come to me directly, and I would then send them back to Tolimir, who would then maybe include his proposals and send them back to me, or to the commander, who would then reach the final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, General. And we'll get to this in a little more detail later, but you'll recall that you have been shown many of these convoy requests for 1995, and you've identified the initials and signatures of various members of the Main Staff; General Mladic, General Tolimir, General Gvero. So given that -- can you explain to us -- in 1995, yes, we know about this civilian commission, but did the Main Staff remain involved in this process, from what you've seen regarding the initials and the various things that you have identified that we'll get to later?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: By using the documents, the request, and the approvals or non-approvals, I reached the conclusion that the commission was functioning throughout 1995, especially when I was in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what was the Main Staff involvement with that? Because, as I think you'll agree, you noticed Mladic is making proposals, and Tolimir's initials, Gvero's initials on these requests that were made during the time of the commission, so can you describe what involvement the Main Staff still had in this process, based on what you've reviewed, and your knowledge, of course?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, one correction. General Mladic wasn't the one making proposals. He was the one reaching decisions. And the documents show that he very often would return a request either by the UNPROFOR or the commission to Tolimir and Gvero, asking them for their opinion. In several instances, I could see that Tolimir would say, Yes, and Gvero, No, on the request, or the other way around, and then after that you would see Mladic's initials with his decision. So he would either approve Tolimir's or Gvero's proposal, but Mladic was the one who would have the final say. He would never issue proposals to his subordinates, but he was asking them for opinions. But the commission was functioning throughout 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So who had final control, the commission or Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The final control was in the hands of the army, Mladic, at check-points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So now we can -- let's look at the bigger picture. And you've always talked about seven assistants, and so if we look at the next series of boxes and count from -- well, if we -- let's go backwards from right to left, starting with the Administration of the Air Force. We have, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, ending with you, as the Chief of the Main Staff, and all your staff administrations under you. So are those the seven assistants that you spoke of?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me explain. The Main Staff, as an entity, had five sectors and two administrations. The five sectors had assistant commanders at its head. One was the staff sector, my sector. Then Sector for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs; that was General Gvero's sector. Then I can see here the next one is Logistics, General Djukic. The following one is Sector for Organisation, mobilisation, and Personnel Affairs. In 1995, it was General Petar Skrbic. Sector for Intelligence and Security Affairs, General Tolimir, throughout the war. And we have two administrations that are directly linked up with the commander. One is the Administration for Planning -- Development and Planning, headed by General-Major Evo Tomic; and Administration for Air Force and Air Defence, headed by Major-General Jovo Maric [Realtime translation read in error "Mladic"]. So the five sectors and two administrations, they were directly linked up to the commander, and the chiefs of these sectors and administrations were commanders' assistants. Other administrations were linked up with their chiefs of sectors. For instance, the 1st Administration for Operations and Planning, that's General Miletic's administration, they're linked up to me. For General Tolimir, there were two, also, administrations; namely, Intelligence and Security. That was Beara. Do you want to hear about any other administrations or sectors?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to make one correction for the transcript. Page 41, line 7, I read there the name headed by General Mladic, but in fact it was General Maric, the chief of the Administration for Air Force and Air Defence. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 38, lines 23 through to 25, you have referred to Operation Parachute. Can you just explain what that operation involved? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Operation Parachute was supply of humanitarian aid into enclaves by air-lifts or, rather, by parachuting the materiel in the planes that I think were sent on the basis of a decision reached by the Security Council. The idea was to provide humanitarian aid in a secure way, but I later started thinking that the idea also included parachuting in materiel that was not allowed, because the materiels were thrown out of the planes at a very high altitude, at 10.000 metres. Some of the cases fell into the territory of Republika Srpska, in two or three cases. And were we opened each one of those crates, we found, for instance, in one occasion, in the area between Srebrenica and Milici, we found ammunition for machine-guns, 7. -- and -- 12.7 millimetres that was packed in bags that allegedly contained flour. But the person who found it said, Well, flour cannot be that heavy. The only thing we could do about it was inform UNPROFOR of such instances. We couldn't order anyone who was packing this not to do that anymore because it was -- the bags were packed somewhere in Germany, but we could inform UNPROFOR about such instances. I'm not sure whether they managed to correct the situation. The operation went on for several months, but I guess because we kept complaining about enclaves being supplied with ammunition, and so on and so forth, they suspended the operation, saying that it was not an efficient way of supplying humanitarian aid, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I seem to recall you saying that the assistant commanders would make proposals through you to -- that you would present to General Mladic. Would those assistant commanders be able to make proposals directly to General Mladic if they so chose, even if you were present?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that we didn't understand each other. The other assistant commanders submitted proposals to the commander. I listened to those proposals and I would take what I believed I would need when I submit my final proposal on the combat use of units. So each one of them would make their proposals directly to the commander. It was another matter that I was listening and that that would help me formulate my own proposals, because proposals were being formulated during the actual meeting. Sometimes, exceptionally, I would prepare them myself, but during the reporting, I would change them. I'm not a bigger expert in security or intelligence than Tolimir, so I would modify my own suggestions according to what he said, for example, in providing support in combat operations. I would not be making up my own proposals. I would be formulating what Tolimir, for example, would bring to the table. So assistant commanders did not make their proposals to me. They made them directly to the commander. I would only listen to that and take them into account or not take them into account when formulating my own proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And what would happen to the proposals? Just to finish the loop on that.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I mentioned that as well. When the proposals were all made, then the commander would usually give a break. I say "usually," but it wouldn't necessarily have to be like that. Perhaps he could be monitoring the proposals right away and formulating the decisions right away. Then he would say, I decided, and then he would dictate the decision. That was one option. But he could also give a break and take the time for himself to reach his decision, and then he would call us again and announce his decisions. In the decision-making system, each one of us assistants would fight for their own proposal; I would, Tolimir, Gvero, all of us would do that. However, when the commander says, I decided, all seven of us would then fervently go about executing that decision, regardless of whether that was in the spirit of our own proposal or not. This was in the spirit of subordination. We had corps commands where the Chief of Staff would propose something, the commander would decide otherwise, but the Chief of Staff would continue to do what he wanted. And then in that case we would abandon/regroup such persons. The Chief of Staff would have to be along the same line as the commander. They would have to respect these rules of subordination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in the event -- let's take the situation where General Tolimir makes a proposal that is adopted by General Mladic, and General Mladic makes an order that's consistent with the proposal and has something to do with the security and intel function. What, if any, responsibility would General Tolimir have in the execution of or monitoring of that order, as I say, if any?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: If Tolimir's proposal was not in line with Mladic's decision, Tolimir would carry out Mladic's decision no matter what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, in a situation where they were both on the same page - Tolimir makes a proposal, Mladic issues an order - how does Tolimir carry it out? What's his responsibility, as the chief of the sector at the Main Staff, for something that would involve the corps, for example?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: He would carry out the commander's decision regardless of whether that was something that corresponded with his proposal or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand. And how would he carry it out? Give us just an idea of just what his responsibilities would be generally. I'm just trying to get a general feeling for the responsibility of any assistant commander whose proposal gets turned into an order.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It states: "Order to the subordinate unit," and it would be -- he would write it in the spirit of the commander's decision, and then he would monitor the execution. I don't know if I was clear enough. If the commander did not accept my proposal, I would execute his decision regardless of the fact that I disagree with it, for example. If he does accept the proposal, then the job is easier for both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's the situation I want to -- I'm asking you about. And you said he, the assistant commander, in this case Tolimir, would monitor the decision. What does that mean, militarily? What's it mean to monitor something?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: To monitor the execution of a decision means seeing if the subordinate unit that was issued the decision was implementing it in the way the commander had decided. If the unit or the subordinate commander was doing something else, it was Tolimir's duty to direct him back to work in the spirit of the commander's decision, with addition orders, explanations, by personally going and telling the commander, You're not doing this in the spirit of the commander's decision, you're making up something of your own. So it is to keep him in the direction or in the course of the commander's decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how long will the execution of that order be monitored by the assistant commander, in this case Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until the assignment is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want you to provide just a little bit of your knowledge and experience on some of these sectors or administrations. The Trial Chamber has heard some information and evidence on some of them, but I just want to get your succinct and brief testimony on these and some information on the chief of the various sectors or administrations I'll be asking you about. So let's, first of all, start with your side, on the left. There, we have it. And you've already spoken a bit about General Miletic as the -- he was the chief of the Administration for Operations and Training; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have already spoken about that he was your deputy and would sometimes replace you, when you weren't there, to chair some of these meetings, but can you basically describe, simply, just in two or three minutes, what his responsibilities were as the chief of operations and training, aside from those that you've already told us?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: His daily duties, as the chief of the administration, were -- and now I'm not speaking about the duties as my deputy -- were to compile and analyse reports from subordinate commands. At the evening meeting, he would state the main problems from the reports by the subordinate commands, and he would give his view as how to resolve each of those problems. He would draft reports and send them to the Supreme Command. He would draft all combat orders, information, notifications relating to the decision of the commander of the previous morning. He would author all the combat documents. In my absence, besides these jobs, he would also carry out the Chief of Staff's daily duties, which were to control the orders being drafted by his administration, signing reports to the Supreme Command, directly address the commander in relation to some problems in the staff or the staff sector. He would be carrying out the day-to-day duties usually conducted by the Chief of Staff when he was there.
