This was his additional duty because, by establishment, he was standing in for the Chief of Staff. This could last up to a period of 30 days. If the Chief of Staff does not return to the Main Staff, there would usually be a way for me to appear at least once a month at the Main Staff in order that we would not have to make any personnel changes in the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell -- how important was that job, the job of the operations officer? You may recall how you described it in the last trial, in the Popovic case.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I said then that an operative in a command or a staff was the soul of that command. All the information comes to him from the subordinate unit, and all the information is dispatched from him to subordinate and superior commands. So this person, in brief, would be like a traffic cop at an intersection where a whole bunch of information was arriving, and he is the one who would be directing this flow of information. He's a person who, at a given command, would know everything or should know everything, including what the commander is doing, what the last soldier in that army is doing, as the person who is carrying out tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I think this is a good time, because you have stated several times that in your absence he would have various other important duties, where were you during most of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: From the 1st of January, 1995, until the end of February, I was in the West, in Drvar. Actually, from the 30th of October, 1994, until the end of February 1995 I was in the West. In early March, I appeared at the Main Staff in order to prepare the annual analysis of the war or the combat readiness of the Army of Republika Srpska. And then from the 6th to the 12th of March I went west again because I was still responsible for that part of the front, following the Bihac operation. Then from the 12th of March until the 3rd of May, I was at the Main Staff. However, I was responsible from the Main Staff to the front around the Sava towards Western Slavonia. And then on the 3rd of May, I transferred to Gradiska in order to organise the defence of Republika Srpska from the direction of the Croatian territory. We're talking about the well-known Croatian Operation Flash. I think that I stayed in the West until the 18th of March. On the 18th of March, I appeared in the Main Staff again, and I was there continuously until the 29th of May. In the meantime, I was conducting defence operations from the aggression of the NATO pact against Republika Srpska. This is the 24th, the 25th, and the 26th of May. And then at repeated intervention of General Tomanic, on the 29th of May I was sent again to the West, to Drvar, because the Muslims had violated the well-known four-month Carter truce, and they crossed again and violated the area of Republika Srpska across the Una River. And the Croats began their offensive against Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serbian Krajina, which was known by the name of Storm. When we're talking about Storm, I think it's incorrect. I tried several times also before this Tribunal and in the media to deny the Croatian assertion that Storm began on the 4th of August, 1995, and was completed on the 5th of August, 1995. Storm began on the 4th of June, 1995, and was completed sometime on October 15th, 1995. It was completed not under the name of Storm, but under the name of Juzni Potez, Southern Flank, but it was the same armed forces formation. From the 29th of May and then until the 15th of October I spent in the West. I arrived a few days before the signing of the Dayton Accords.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you: You say, again, you spent the time between May and October in the West. Could you specify what you mean by that again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was conducting combat actions of the Army of Republika Srpska on the front in the Bosnian Krajina, on the River Una, the Dinara Mountain. That was it. I was conducting the defence actions from Muslims from the Bihac Security Zone and defence from the Croatian Army from the Livanjsko Polje and the Golije-Staretina-Sator-Cincar-Vitorog Mountains. Perhaps I skipped over a hill or a mountain, maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to come back to an issue we discussed earlier, about the meetings of the Main Staff in the morning and in the evening. Where did these meetings take place during that time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meetings were held at the Operations Centre of the Main Staff. This was the largest room in the prefabricated huts where we were located. As I said, the meetings were attended by the assistant commanders, if they were there. If any of them was not there, their deputy would be there. And the leading leadership team would also attend these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where were these prefabricated huts located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These prefabricated huts were in Crna Rijeka, some nine kilometres north-east of Han Pijesak. At a slope, we found two such huts on the 19th of May, when we got there. During the war, we built another one, the third one. It was a small area, because we worked and slept in these huts. And just to show how small a space it was, suffice it to say that General Mladic and I shared an office. If Mladic was there, I wasn't, and if I was there, he wasn't. Usually that's how it worked. But we shared an office in order to save space or make best use of the space. Other than the huts, we also had an underground command post which was 1 kilometre away from the huts. It was dug out. I think it was 471 metres underground, under Veliki Zejg [phoen], where we would go in case of threats of NATO strikes or during NATO strikes. The entire Main Staff would move to this underground command post, which would be able to function for six months, with a number of persons there being 500. It was completely self-sufficient. It was like a small subterranean town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, General Milovanovic, I see here that from May 1995 until October, the 15th of October, 1995, you left and went east. You were in charge of the battle against the Croats, which was fighting against the Republika Srpska and the Krajina Republic. The battle or the fighting had actually started in June of 1995. And at the same time, if I look at the organisation chart of the Main Staff of the VRS in July of 1995, you are the deputy commander of the Main Staff. How are you able to reconcile your two jobs, i.e., as deputy Chief of Staff and in charge of the military operation against the Croats to the east of the country in 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it's the west of the territory, not the east. I was deputy commander for military operations, translated into NATO terminology. My duty was to plan operations and, if the commander ordered so, to carry out operations. In practice, this is how it was. I would plan or my sector would plan an operation, and the commander usually would allocate me, as the main planner, to begin the execution of the operation because I had the right to change things if something was not going right. It's not easy to predict the course of combat. So if something does not proceed according to plan initially, the plan that I drafted and that the commander or the supreme commander approved, then I can change things immediately. On the ground, I'm not going to send one brigade, but two; instead of two, perhaps three. So I was the person who could change the initial plan as the operations went along. If the operation, in the beginning, proceeded quite well, then the commander would leave me there to complete it. But the command principle in the Main Staff was this: If, in an operation, there are two or more corps taking part, the operation is under the command of the commander of the Main Staff. However, if a sector of the front, because the front of Republika Srpska was about 700 kilometres long and 150 kilometres wide, if operations at corps level are being executed in another place, then the commander usually stays where the bulk of the fighting is and then he would assign me or some other assistant of his to that other sector of the front in order to conduct the operation. And this time, this was in the West. First of all, I spent late 1994 and early 1995 in the West, executing that initial strike towards Bihac. I said that the 5th Muslim Corps violated Carter's truce, and beginning from the 13th of January, 1995, they started slowly eating away at our territory. They crossed the Una River, violated the truce, and by the 12th of February had taken up part of the territory on Grmec Mountain. They had retaken that part of the territory. I made a new counter-strike plan towards Bihac. The plan was approved by the Supreme Command. The commander of the 2nd Krajina Corps asked twice that I personally get to that part of the front. I don't know what the corps commander's motivation was for that. I refused to do it the first time. This was in early May, when I was in Gradiska fighting against -- Flash. When I returned to the staff, on the 25th of May the corps commander sent an ultimatum -- a request to the Main Staff that I would have to come to that sector of the front. Otherwise, he would leave Bijecevica [phoen] Mountain. And so I had made some reinforcements at Krupa Na Uni before that. Before that, I had told General Mladic and Supreme Commander Karadzic that I didn't want to do this because I did not want to be tied down, as the Chief of Staff, to one sector of the front of Republika Srpska. But General Tolimir, who is present here, convinced me to accept and to agree to that summons because I knew the corps the best and I understood the Serbian Army of the Krajina, which was acting in co-ordination very well, and I also was very familiar with that particular area. And seeing that it was no longer a joke and that this commander was being very persistent, I accepted the summons and I went on the 29th of May. On the 4th of June, I initiated the counter-strike, the second one towards Bihac. On the Croatian side, there was no threat from that direction. I even took some artillery weapons from the Glamoc front, transferred them to the Bihac front. In the morning, we began, on the 4th, on Sunday at 4.00 a.m., and in about two hours we had broken through the Muslim front towards Bihac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Witness, for having specified what your military action to the West involved. But you remember a while ago we discussed the collegium of commanders. Whilst you were in the West, did that mean that you were not taking part or were not a member of the collegium of commanders at that time? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't attend their meetings and did not. There was no need for it because I had received my task at the Western Front. It was a long-term task to repel the Croatian Operation Storm. Therefore, no needs were required on my end. The only thing that happened was when I asked for reinforcements by telegram or telephone. I simply wasn't present at the meetings and there was no need for me to. I was only present there when I was particularly called by the commander, when analyses of combat readiness for the previous year were done. I was also at the Main Staff once when we saw General Zivanovic, commander of the Drina Corps, off because he retired. The custom was that all generals got together on such occasions. I arrived on the 19th of July. We saw him off on the 20th. And on the 22nd, I was already back in Drvar. So this was the only exception. Yes. So basically there were only two interruptions in the whole period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. My last question now. When you were not present, was someone appointed to act on your behalf when you were not on the spot where the operation was taking place? Was a deputy commander, an acting deputy commander, ever appointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was replaced by General Miletic, per establishment. My absence from the Main Staff up to 30 days did not require any new orders for Miletic. He would simply pick up where I left it off in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you receive a specific order from General Mladic authorising you to command that -- the operation you've described from May 29th in the West?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I received an order from General Mladic to go westward to execute that counter-strike against Bihac. I began doing so, but on the same day the Croats attacked the VRS from Livanjsko Polje through the villages of Peulje. Their aim, and that is something I did not learn in the course of that day, but in the next following days, was not the RS. Their goal was to occupy Knin. They were unable to do that from the direction of Dalmacija, perhaps because of the lie of the land, so they came up with this idea of engaging in a comprehensive manoeuvre through the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, thank you. Thank you. And I just wanted to clarify that you had been given a command position for the Western Front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, I have to interrupt you. We have a problem with the transcript in e-court again. It's not working at the moment. I hope it's working in LiveNote. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Registrar makes the proposal that we have our break now because we have so many problems now with the microphone, with the e-court, the e-court record, and some other problems. I think we should have our break now, and during the break everything should be resolved. If this is convenient for everybody, we should have our break now and resume 20 minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we had left off and I think you'd clarified that General Mladic had actually given you a command position on the Western Front on the end of May 1995. And you have explained this a bit, and the policy of sending out a general from the Main Staff if there was two corps involved, and other things on that same topic, but, practically, throughout the war, were you and other assistants from the Main Staff sent out to take command positions or important positions in the various battle-fronts of the war?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was standard practice of the commander to dispatch his assistants, be it as commanders or monitors, to control. On one occasion, he sent General Gvero to the Olovo front, between Sarajevo and Olovo, where Operation Ring was being executed, and that ought to be distinguished from Operation Ring 2. Gvero was in command then, and it included parts of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps and some headquarters support units, such as the 65th Protection Regiment. It means that there were more units than one single corps, and Gvero was in command. I can't recall, off the cuff, anyone else being in command of operations. Sorry, yes, he also sent the then artillery chief, Colonel Masala, to Gornji Podrinje. He commanded the temporary formations of the operations and tactical group. The commander authorised him to command those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And the Trial Chamber has learned, as we all have, that the assistant commanders, well, at all levels, brigades, corps, and the main staffs, have -- are experts in their field, be it artillery, as you've just mentioned, or General Gvero in morale, legal, religious; or General Tolimir in intel and security. Can you explain, as a general, how it could be that a person that's an expert in a particular field would be effective in command or in monitoring a significant battle-front?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand which expert you had in mind, because in the army there are two types of experts. There are those who are versed in general military matters, that is, commanders; and then there are specialists, such as Tolimir, who was a specialist for intelligence and security, or Gvero for morale issues. Some people are both. By virtue of becoming general, irrespective of one's specialty, the person is capable of exercising general military command. A colonel -- a quarter-master officer can also be in charge of commands pursuant to orders. He can also deal with general military issues. As it happened in our army, we had six brigade commanders who were traffic specialists. We also had four of them from the Financial Branch, and yet they were in charge of brigades. We also had six communications men who were in commanding positions. They had nothing to do with infantry or artillery, and yet they were successful brigade commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And you've outlined the basic time-periods where you were away from the Main Staff. And in preparation of the last trial, did you have an opportunity to review the reports from the Main Staff to the Presidency and see whose name they went to the president in?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I reviewed all the reports sent in 1995. They were sent from the Main Staff to the supreme commander, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And whose names did those go out under?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them were signed by General Miletic, as my deputy, but he signed them incorrectly as standing for the Chief of Staff. However, he did not stand for me. It is a strictly legal category. He replaced me instead. So he should have signed it differently, as "on behalf of the Chief of Staff." However, he automatically just put down "standing in for." When I followed some testimony here, I realised that Colonel Trkulja, who was the author of those reports, recognised his mistake. He said he did so because he wasn't attentive enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did your review of all of those reports for 1995, and noticing your name or General Miletic's name, did that help you at all in putting together what days you were in the Main Staff and what days you weren't?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I returned to the Main Staff, I did not read such documents that were of limited, temporal value. I had no time to go back and study everything. I'm referring to those reports that I was expected to sign at those times when I was in the Main Staff. The things which expired is something I didn't bother with. The most important things were told me by Miletic himself. There was simply no time for me to leaf through the archives. It's a different matter that I read them later on here in this building. However, that was a number of years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that's my question. When you were able to review them in this building, does the fact that your name was on some of them throughout 1995 and Miletic's was on most of them, did that help give you any indication of when you might have -- or when you were in the Main Staff and when you were not? I'm talking after the fact now.

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part, yes, because I was unable to recollect all those individual segments as to when I took him to the Main Staff. But if I went by my signatures, then most of the time I could tell at what times I was at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you very briefly explain to us: You've said that this term "standing in" is, I think, an official or formal term and that it was not used correctly by Trkulja, so can you tell us, very briefly, what the formal "standing in" means and how it comes about?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The easiest way for me to explain would be by using an example of a command role. Say a brigade commander falls ill and abandons the unit. Up to 30 days, he is replaced by his establishment deputy, that is to say, his Chief of Staff. If the commander's absence is longer than 30 days, the superior officer to the brigade, that is to say, the corps commander, appoints a person to stand in for him by virtue of an order. The person so appointed has all of the authority the brigade commander enjoyed. Standing in, under the then law, could last for a maximum period of six months. Following that, there is either a new order on standing in or a new person is appointed to act as brigade commander or another order is issued to appoint the person standing in thus far as brigade commander. So "standing in" is a legal category. It also entails a change of salary. And one simply takes on all the responsibilities of a commander. If simply acting on behalf of someone, one would not have such duties and obligations, and this was mainly done parallel to one's own duties. Perhaps it is strange why Miletic was not accorded this status when I was absent for more than six months, but that was because I was at the front-lines. I was not outside the VRS. Irrespective of where I was at the front-line, I maintain my position of Chief of Staff, and Miletic only stood in. I wasn't incapacitated, I wasn't ill, but I was engaged in another staff task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I think that is all I want to ask you about for the operations and training part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You've just now explained what happens 30 days and onwards. What -- how is it described or called before the 30 days lapses? What is the person who acts or who stands in, in that position described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe I explained the term "standing in for." Due to the physical inability of someone to perform his or her duties, a person is appointed to stand in for that person. If someone is attending another task as part of the same armed forces, then that person is replaced by his next most superior person in his organ. Miletic was the most senior person in the staff sector, and he replaced me. He was supposed to sign by stating "for." So "Chief of Staff Manojlo Milovanovic," that would be in the signature block, and then Miletic was supposed to sign "for," and then he put his own name under it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I think I was not clear in my question, and this is because I can't highlight where I'm trying to focus. In your explanation, in the explanation that you've given just now, in my understanding it relates to somebody who stands in for you after 30 days. My question is: What is the person standing in for you up to 30 days described as? Is it the same? Say, for example, somebody is standing in for you for two weeks or three weeks or 25 days. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not the same. "Standing in for" is a legal category which requires an order. Replacing someone for a limited period of time requires no written order, but things simply continue as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, we have not the -- there is now French interpretation on the English channel. Now it's working. In this period of 30 days, the deputy just is in the position of the person of the commander for whom he is the deputy, without a specific term you are using? He's just the deputy, is that correct, in this period of 30 days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, to put it in the briefest way possible, he acts on behalf of the person who is absent. Miletic performed my duties in the staff in my absence, such as reviewing correspondence, drafting reports, receiving subordinate reports, and all the other daily tasks. If key decisions need to be made, he had no right to propose anything to the commander. He could always get in touch with me. And if the commander needed me personally, he could always summon me to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just one more thing to help clarify it in my mind. You've described that Miletic was replacing you or acting on your behalf, but those words don't need to be placed in the signature block, is that what you're saying, just as long as the "for" word is mentioned, the "za" word?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And those terms that I just mentioned are not formal, legal military terms, they just describe the situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: It seems I have to repeat. If someone is standing in for another, he or she has the same rights as the person he is acting for, or standing in for, excuse me. If Miletic stood in for me, then he could exercise my powers. However, if he was only replacing me, if the word "for" was to be affixed to his signature, he did not enjoy the same right as I did. He could only deal with the daily routine tasks so to avoid the staff coming at a standstill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. I think we understand. And so let's move on from that part to the next sector, which is the Sector for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs, headed by General Gvero. And can you very briefly describe what General Gvero's job was in the Main Staff, especially in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, including 1995, General Gvero was tasked with raising the morale of the VRS, maintaining it, that is to say, preventing the morale from deteriorating among the ranks. That was one thing. Another thing that he was also in charge were religious affairs. That is to say, he was there to provide conditions for the troops to attend religious ceremonies, et cetera. He was also to liaise with the church institutions. Perhaps Mr. Tolimir would be better placed to explain that. In any case, he was supposed to make it possible for the officers and soldiers to perform their religious rites, et cetera. He was also an assistant commander for legal affairs, which means that he had to keep an eye on the lawfulness of the work of the military courts, and he was also in charge of establishing them. This lasted until sometime in 1994, when the military courts were no longer under the competence of the Main Staff and the army. They were returned to their proper place, which is under the authority of the Ministry of Defence. However, Gvero continued monitoring the work of the military courts, although he no longer had to under the law. He was in charge of controlling their work, and he was responsible to the commander for the work of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, personally, did he exhibit any religious affinity or did he have any religious position in any religion, General Gvero, that is?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about his religious affiliation, but I do know that in our political school he taught Marxism, which is a theory completely opposite to religion. I have not noticed any changes in his views during the war, although it was his duty to provide conditions for the army members to do their religious things. I don't think he was an atheist, but I've never seen him pray. There is a story that I can recount. The archbishop of the Serbian Orthodox Church visited the Main Staff, Mr. Paulin [phoen]. I was not present in the Main Staff. And in the underground command post there was an office of the Chief of Staff where the Chief of Staff would work, but where also meetings were being held. And when I joined them in the afternoon, while the archbishop was still there, I found in my room a religious painting and a candle, and I asked General Mladic who was it who placed this here. And he responded, Well, it was the archbishop, and the proposal came from General Gvero, who was in charge on religious issues. And this office, this room actually, is a very busy room. People yell, make phone calls, and I told General Mladic, Well, since the candle is here in my room, let General Gvero properly light it up. But he didn't know how, so I would say that General Gvero was not a person who was well versed in religious things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How about General Tolimir; did you ever see him exhibit religious beliefs or religious practices?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I haven't seen him. And as far as his knowledge about religion, well, on one occasion when I was about to enter a church in Vlasenica where something was going on, there was a procession about to start, and we needed to discuss something, and the bishop told us, If you want, you can find a quiet corner in the church. And then he made a joke, If the general wants to enter the church. And I returned the joke by saying, I will go with the commander wherever he tells me. But upon entering the church, we saw General Tolimir at the entrance, and he told me, You're not supposed to bring in any weapons. I had a Hekler on me. I didn't know anything about these things, and I handed over the Hekler. But I also had four bombs in my uniform. So, in effect, I did bring weapons into the church. But I never saw Tolimir praying to God, and he cursed as much as everyone else in the Main Staff. So, no, during the war, in the time we almost lived together, I did not notice any special religious proclivities on his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Going back to General Gvero, can you describe his influence with General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I spoke about this during my last testimony in 2007. Gvero did not have any special influence on General Mladic. On the contrary, General Mladic, up until the time I went to the Western Front, often -- well, you see, the two of us would often have conversations privately, outside of the staff. We would walk around the huts, and he would always tell me, Let Gvero be; he's a politician. I also said just a moment ago that Gvero was the officer in charge of the Operation Ring in Olovo or at the Olovo Front-Line, and they were having a hard time. It was winter-time, and Mladic sent me on one occasion there, and I was escorted by one of Gvero's officers, Vidoje Magazin, his name was, and he was a colonel, I think. And he told me, Go and see what Gvero is doing, and if what he is doing is not efficient, suspend all the activities until the end of the winter. And I got there, I found Gvero there at the forward command post. He briefed me on the situation. It was too much snow for any movement. And I ordered Gvero to change the status to defence status, to take his forces in, and I don't think the operation was ever resumed. So, no, General Mladic was not under influence of General Gvero. Only after my arrival from the West Front, which was in second half of October, whenever we were not really busy in the staff, Mladic would go for walks, usually with me, around the Main Staff deployment area or he would go to General Tolimir. They knew each other from Knin, so I wasn't paying that much attention to that. But after my return, Mladic would not choose me as his walking companion, but Gvero and Beara. And I was at first a little bit sore about that, but that was after Dayton, so it wasn't very important anymore. I don't know whether Gvero had some influence on Mladic at the time. I know that Gvero, on one occasion, told me -- after the Dayton Accords and after a minor stroke that General Mladic had suffered, Gvero told me, when we were on our own, the two of us, he said, I had a stroke, and I'm not sure sometimes whether two plus two makes four. Tolimir also had one, so you should not rely on him too much. And I apologise to Mr. Tolimir now. He added, You're probably the only one who's unaffected. And he told me about Gvero the following thing, Well, it's the end of the war, so he's looking for some place where he can fit in into the political structures. And Mladic at the time started insulting and cursing the members of staff. He told me, Well, if you see me doing something like that, you're always next to me at the table, then just kick me under the table. And I was pleased to hear that, because his behaviour started causing problems in the staff. And after this conversation, we went out. And there was a table there, and quite a few officers used to sit there, and there was a sheep that came that was lame, and there was a veterinarian colonel there who Mladic asked about, Why is this sheep lame? And the officer said, Well, this is a sheep from Kalinovik, and the climate here is different from there, and they're having difficulties. And Mladic, who was from the area of Kalinovik, started cursing the colonel, and I kicked him with my boot. But then he said, What I told you earlier is not really in effect anymore. But I don't think, to come back to your question, that Gvero had any special influence on Mladic. I don't think he had that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I didn't -- I'm sorry, I wasn't, perhaps, clear. I didn't mean special influence. But you may remember, when you were asked questions in the last trial and describing your -- in providing proposals and guidance and advice to General Mladic, you described yourself as the first among equals and something about all the assistants had influence. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember saying that I was the first among equals. And the question was put to me by Mr. Krgovic, the Defence lawyer, and he asked me whether Gvero had been Mladic's right hand, and my response was that according to establishment I was General Mladic's right hand. If he had additional right hands, that was his thing, not mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So my question about influence really has to do with advice, proposals, whether Mladic listened to you and acted on you in that kind of a context. So if -- can you describe what you meant? When you said "first among equals," that all the assistant commanders had influence, what did you mean by that? Could you explain that a little more fully, but as briefly as you can?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: "First among equals" means that I, in addition to being assistant commander for staff affairs, I'm also deputy commander. In other words, I have a title that other assistant commanders don't have. That's the issue. They were all part of the Main Staff, but I was in charge of the staff itself. That means first among equals. I didn't mean first among equals that Mladic would listen to most. Mladic appreciated my proposals, but my role was to summarise all the proposals of other assistant commanders. And, of course, Mladic was listening also to the proposals of all of his assistant commanders, including the Chief of Financial Administration Colonel Tomic. General Mladic devoted due attention to all of us when we were making proposals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you and the assistant commanders and General Mladic work as a team?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Mladic treated his entire staff as one team. All seven assistant commanders were a part of a team. But he would also do that on an individual basis, one on one. Especially when issues relating to our specialties were at stake, it would be one-on-one discussions. For instance, with me when combat operations were in charge; with Tolimir when security and intelligence affairs were at stake; with Gvero about morale and legal affairs. He didn't care much about religious parts. With Djukic in relation to logistics, and so on and so forth. He didn't make any distinctions, at least to my knowledge, between us in that sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me go over now to the Sector for Security and Intelligence. And the Trial Chamber has heard a lot about that from the brigade level, the corps level, even the Main Staff level, but can you tell us, briefly, what General Tolimir's job practically consisted of? What was his job throughout the war, and especially in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: The task of Tolimir's sector, the Intelligence and Security Sector, and therefore of Tolimir himself, because he was chief of the sector, was Intelligence and Counter-Intelligence Service activities; namely, gathering information about the enemy and prevention of any leaks of information. He had two assistants. One would collect information, that was Intelligence Administration, headed by Colonel Salapura. So it was Salapura's task to gather information by analysing daily reports, media, by getting reports from his subordinated intelligence officers from lower units like corps and brigades. He also had to organise so-called forcible gathering of information by moving combat deployment and similar activities. In other words, there are two types of gathering of information, active and passive. The other administration under Tolimir's administration or command was the Security Administration headed by Colonel Beara, and their task was to make sure that military information at the disposal of Republika Srpska and about the Republika Srpska Army would not leak to the enemy. This was something done in the passive manner, so to speak. That's, at least, how I understood it. But part of the active part of these duties, interrogating prisoners of war, securing them by using military police and the such. So Tolimir's sector was in charge of intelligence and counter-intelligence affairs; in other words, gathering information and making sure that information about us does not leak to the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. You just said that: "The other administration under Tolimir's administration or command ..." So is it fair to say that General Tolimir was in command of the Intelligence Administration and the Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Can you describe General Tolimir's relationship with General Mladic? And, first of all, on a professional basis. For example, did they -- like you've described yours with General Mladic, how you saw things differently, but your temperaments fit, how would you describe the professional relationship that you saw during the war years between Generals Mladic and Tolimir, and, again, especially in 1995, if there were any changes?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't speak about the relationship between Mladic and Tolimir for the duration of the entire war. I cannot speak specifically about 1995 because I did not spend all of the year with them there. But upon my return, I did not notice there had been any major changes. I already told you that I made a mistake on the occasion when Tolimir was introduced to us by Mladic, when I showed that I believed Tolimir was a Slovene, but they were together in Knin and they had maybe nine months or up to a year of joint combat experience together. They knew more about war than those among us who joined in on the 12th of May. I know that they would consult with each other often. For instance, I make a proposal, or something like that, and before making a decision, Mladic would say, I'll go and talk to Toso, as we used to call Tolimir, and see what he thinks. Whenever Mladic had to do something, he would always ask the assistant commanders to analyse the matter and to, in a way, give a green light to him in relation to his intentions. And on one occasion we got a letter General Mladic wrote to General Wahlgren, who was the commander of the UNPROFOR forces for former Yugoslavia, who had his headquarters in Zagreb. So Mladic read this letter out to us from his manuscript, asking for our input, whether something needs to be removed or put in, and the letter was drafted in a manner of a commander, without nice turns of phrase or political balancing. It was rather arrogant and sounded like an ultimatum, Unless you do this, I will do that, and so on and so forth. And I remember Gvero and Tolimir making comments about, Why didn't you phrase it like this or like that? As I was listening to that, I was getting more and more agitated. I don't know whether Tolimir remembers that. We were sitting around those tables between the huts, and I told everyone, You are telling the commander this is not right, instead of giving a proposal as how it should be drafted. I don't know what happened next with the letter, whether Mladic changed it or not. I can't remember that anymore. But what I'm trying to say is that both Tolimir and Gvero had the courage to criticise Mladic. In other words, General Mladic, although he was the commander, he viewed things democratically and would listen to proposals by others. We in the Main Staff knew that General Mladic trusted General Tolimir a lot, and I didn't mind that at all. And that's the reason why I told the Trial Chamber in the previous trial about if there were any other right hands, it's his thing. He had trust in -- he trusted Tolimir and he trusted Beara, and I never understood why Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You stated that a part of the responsibility of the Intel and Security Sector, General Tolimir, would be the prevent of any leaks of information. Can you tell us what that means?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: For instance, if we're preparing an operation, Tolimir's task or his sector's task, not objective, was to make sure that the enemy would not find out about the operation before we start with the operation itself. In other words, to cover up the intentions of the VRS, to make the enemy believe or to make the enemy reach wrong conclusions. In accordance to what Napoleon had said, If you see the enemy making mistakes, assist him in making mistakes. And I think the sector was rather successful in its task until, of course, the Logistics Service got involved, because then they would start making requisitions or getting the materiel, and then, of course, it would come out, Oh, yes, because the VRS is planning an attack against Zuc. But, in any case, their main task was to hide the intentions and all elements involving the functioning of the army. The enemy should not have found out anything our intentions before we hit them. There was one thing that they failed to uncover. The Intelligence Service did not inform me about preparations of the Croatian Army for their Operation Storm. They informed me about Operation Flash, but I didn't know anything about Operation Storm until it started. And it is impossible; they couldn't have linked things up, because Croats were bringing their forces from Rijeka, Bjelovar, and Varazdin, and Osijek, Omis, Split, bringing them all to the area of Glamoc. They had 75.000 troops there, and it's impossible for the Intelligence Service not to have noticed that, and they should have told me about it. Instead, they let me attack the Muslim forces in the area of Bihac, and that is one thing that will remain on their souls forever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you recall how you, just in a few words, described General Tolimir's job in the Popovic trial?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did review the transcript before coming here and partially listened to the CD recording, but I'm not sure what context you are referring to, in terms of me describing Tolimir. I think I said more or less the same thing; perhaps not in so many words, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I recall some -- one of us - it may have been a Defence attorney - asking you if someone was General Mladic's eyes and ears. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was Counsel Zivanovic's question. He asked me whether Tolimir was Mladic's eyes and ears, and I said that this was precisely Tolimir's duty. He was in charge of gathering intelligence. Those would be Mladic's ears. He also prevented any leaks of information from the VRS, meaning he was there to open Mladic's eyes. Tolimir, being an intelligence officer, was supposed to act as the ears and eyes of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And aside from this failure for you to get good intelligence on the Western Front, how good was Tolimir -- General Tolimir at his job?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've just got five more minutes. Could you briefly explain how effective General Tolimir was at accomplishing the tasks that you've described and how intelligent he was in going about that work?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: General Tolimir, in his own sector, did not hire his assistants, the chief of the Intelligence Administration and the Security Administration, to the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: He did not involve them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ... in his work to the extent he should have, I believe, because he always knew more than the two of them did. However, throughout the war, General Tolimir worked on the relationship of the VRS and foreign militaries, such as UNPROFOR, since we did not have separate bodies to deal with it. He accompanied General Mladic at all negotiations and talks, be it at home or abroad. I think he became exhausted in liaising with UNPROFOR generals, albeit it was justified. All contact with other armed forces went through General Tolimir. I think he was quite successful in doing so, and this relieved Mladic and myself to a great extent. He had a feel for diplomacy. Another thing: General Tolimir wrote down everything. I don't think I'll exaggerate if I told you that he had his note-book even at lunchtime, and we always teased him, asking him, Why do you write so much? And he would always say, It's for posterity; it should remain for history's sake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did his responsible for the prevention of leaks of important military information extend to preventing leaks to the international community and the public media?

utterances.speaker: MANOJLO MILOVANOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't know what it was he was doing vis-à-vis the international community. He was in charge of preventing any leaks, including anyone, not just the enemy, but anyone else who wasn't supposed to now. That is what "prevention of leaks" means. Information must not leave the organisation. If the enemy, the Muslims or Croats, are not supposed to receive a certain piece of information, it meant that the foreigners were not there to receive it either, because then they would pass it on to our enemy. I don't know whether they ever passed information on our enemy to us. To the extent of my contact with them, that was not my experience. But I do know that the information I gave them they regularly conveyed to the Muslims and Croats. When Mladic or I spoke on the phone, Tolimir was always there tugging at our sleeves, mostly Mladic's, saying, They're eavesdropping; they're intercepting; don't say that. I had occasion to listen to a tape including a conversation between Mladic and a Colonel Vukovic, telling him to fire at the Presidency building and to hit the Muslims hard, and then Mladic also says, All right, all right, Tolimir, just let me be. So he was probably there, telling him not to say such things. Later on, you could hear that particular conversation. At Radio Sarajevo, for half a year they would regularly start their broadcast of the day with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, General. It's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. We have to adjourn for the day, and we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom. Please be reminded that there is no permission for you to have contact with either party about the content of your testimony here in this trial. We adjourn.
